person.name: Antoni_Gaudí
person.summary: Antoni Gaudí was a Catalan architect whose buildings combined structural experimentation, craft, religious imagery, and forms drawn from nature. Working mainly in Barcelona, he designed the Sagrada Família, Park Güell, Casa Batlló, Casa Milà, and other defining works of Catalan Modernisme.

conclusion: Antoni Gaudí's Sagrada Família remains under construction in Barcelona, where architects and craftspeople continue work from his surviving models, drawings, and structural ideas. Casa Batlló, Casa Milà, Park Güell, and other buildings by Gaudí remain in use as homes, museums, and public sites. Seven of his works are listed as UNESCO World Heritage Sites.

events.date_note: Gaudí's birthplace is disputed between Reus and Riudoms in the Baix Camp district
events.title: Birth in Baix Camp
events.description: Antoni Gaudí is born into the Baix Camp coppersmith household of Francesc Gaudí i Serra and Antònia Cornet i Bertran. He is the youngest of their five children. He is baptized the next day at Sant Pere Apòstol in Reus as Antoni Plàcid Guillem Gaudí i Cornet.

Baix Camp.explanation: Baix Camp is a district in the province of Tarragona, in southern Catalonia. Reus and Riudoms are neighboring municipalities within the district.

events.title: Moves to Barcelona
events.description: In 1868 Antoni Gaudí moves from Reus to Barcelona to study teaching at the Convent del Carme. There he shares an interest in [[utopian socialism|utopian socialism]] with fellow students Eduard Toda i Güell and Josep Ribera i Sans. The three plan to restore Poblet Monastery as a cooperative community.

images.caption: Former portal of Barcelona’s Convent del Carme
images.creator: Joaquimet

utopian socialism.explanation: Utopian socialism was a 19th-century tradition that proposed planned, cooperative communities as alternatives to existing social and economic systems. Gaudí and his fellow students discussed applying such ideas to the restoration of Poblet Monastery.

events.title: Studies Architecture
events.description: In 1873, Antoni Gaudí studied architecture at the Llotja School and the Barcelona Higher School of Architecture in Barcelona. He supported himself by drawing plans for architects and builders, including Leandre Serrallach, Joan Martorell, Emili Sala Cortés, Francisco de Paula del Villar y Lozano, and Josep Fontserè.
involved_people: Francisco de Paula del Villar y Lozano

images.caption: Main entrance of Barcelona’s Llotja School
images.creator: Alma1954

events.title: Qualifies as Architect
events.description: In 1878 Antoni Gaudí receives his architectural qualification from the Barcelona Higher School of Architecture. Director Elies Rogent approves it despite Gaudí’s uneven academic results. Gaudí shares the news with his friend Llorenç Matamala.
events.background:
The qualification came at the end of years divided between study and compulsory service in Barcelona’s infantry regiment. Gaudí served as a military administrator from 1875 to 1878. Poor health placed him on sick leave for most of that period, which allowed him to continue his architectural studies. The same health problems kept him out of the Third Carlist War.

In 1876, while he was still completing his training, Gaudí lost his mother and his brother Francesc. Francesc had just qualified as a physician. Gaudí also supported his studies by working as a draftsman for architects and builders.

background_images.caption: Insurrección carlista.—Sorpresa de Reus por la partida de Francesch.
background_images.creator: Josep Lluis Pellicer

events.title: Meets Eusebi Güell
events.description: At the 1878 Paris World’s Fair, Antoni Gaudí displays a showcase he designed for the glove manufacturer Comella. Eusebi Güell sees the work and becomes Gaudí’s patron.

images.caption: Paris pavilion at the 1878 World Fair
images.creator: Roch-Reigner (creator) Scott, P. K. (creator)

events.title: Receives Casa Vicens Commission
events.description: In 1878, stockbroker Manuel Vicens i Montaner commissioned Antoni Gaudí to design a summer house in Barcelona’s Gràcia district. Gaudí created a colorful residence using ceramic tile, brickwork, and wrought ironwork.

events.title: Takes Over Sagrada Família
events.description: In 1883 Antoni Gaudí takes charge of the Sagrada Família in Barcelona after Francisco de Paula del Villar leaves the project following disagreements with Joan Martorell. Martorell advises Josep Maria Bocabella, the project’s promoter. Gaudí replaces Villar’s design based on medieval Gothic forms with his own design.
involved_people: Francisco de Paula del Villar y Lozano
events.background:
The project had begun with a 1877 commission from the Associació de Devots de Sant Josep. Only the crypt had been built under Villar’s Neo-Gothic scheme. Gaudí inherited that completed underground portion and an unfinished church above it.

Martorell was offered the commission before Gaudí. He declined the work and recommended Gaudí. The church became Gaudí’s magnum opus.

background_images.caption: Barcelona - Crypt of La Sagrada Família - 1900-1906
background_images.creator: Txllxt TxllxT

events.title: Builds Casa Calvet
events.description: In 1898, Antoni Gaudí designed Casa Calvet in Barcelona for Pere Màrtir Calvet, a textile manufacturer. The building combined offices, apartments, and the owner's residence within a narrow urban site. Barcelona City Council later recognized it as the city's best building of the year in 1900.

events.title: Plans Park Güell
events.description: In 1900, Eusebi Güell hired Antoni Gaudí to design a garden housing development on a hillside in Barcelona. Gaudí laid out roads, terraces, service structures, and shared spaces across the estate for Güell’s planned community.

events.title: Remakes Casa Batlló
events.description: In 1904, textile industrialist Josep Batlló hired Antoni Gaudí to remodel his residence in Barcelona. Gaudí reshaped the façade, interiors, roof, and [[light wells|light wells]] with curving forms, colored glass, ceramic, and ironwork, working with architect Josep Maria Jujol.

light wells.explanation: Light wells are interior shafts or open spaces designed to bring daylight and ventilation into rooms that do not face the street. Gaudí reworked Casa Batlló's light wells as part of the renovation.

events.background: Jujol had met Gaudí through their mutual friend Dr. Santaló. Casa Batlló became their first project together. Jujol decorated the first floor, created the sacras, and added ceramic work to the façade. Gaudí valued Jujol's views and kept him as a collaborator for years afterward.

events.title: Builds Casa Milà
events.description: In 1906 Pere Milà and Roser Segimon commission Antoni Gaudí to design an apartment house in Barcelona. Gaudí gives it a stone exterior with undulating balconies and open interior courtyards. He designs a roofscape of sculptural chimneys and stair towers with Josep Maria Jujol contributing ornamentation.

images.caption: Casa Milà on Passeig de Gràcia
images.creator: Matti Blume

events.title: Builds Colònia Güell Crypt
events.description: In 1908, Antoni Gaudí designed a church for the workers’ colony established by Eusebi Güell at Santa Coloma de Cervelló. In its unfinished crypt, he tested slanting columns, [[catenary arch|catenary arches]], and brick vaults as structural elements.

catenary arch.explanation: A catenary arch follows the curve formed by a freely hanging chain when inverted. Gaudí used this form to distribute structural loads through the arch and reduce the need for external supports.

events.title: Devotes Himself to Sagrada
events.description: In 1915 Antoni Gaudí makes the Sagrada Família his only commission. Josep Maria Jujol, Joan Rubió, Cèsar Martinell, Francesc Folguera, and Josep Francesc Ràfols help carry out work while he develops designs and structural details.

images.caption: Sagrada Família under construction around 1915
images.creator: Templo Expiatorio de la Sagrada Familia

events.background:
A severe economic crisis halted construction in 1915. Gaudí had also lost his niece Rosa in 1912 and his principal collaborator Francesc Berenguer in 1914. His remaining activities centered on Catholic life. In 1916, he attended a Gregorian chant course at the Palau de la Música Catalana.

His work on the church drew together structural research he had pursued from 1910 to 1920. He planned its interior as a forest. Inclined columns divide into branch-like forms and carry interconnected hyperboloid vaults. The columns use double-turn helicoidal shapes based on the forms of tree trunks and branches.

The hyperboloid vaults left openings at their centers and intersections. These openings admitted natural light and created the effect of a starry sky. The segmented arrangement of columns and vaults was designed to carry the building’s forces without buttresses.

background_images.creator: Enfo

background_images.caption: Hyperboloid vaults covering the central nave
background_images.creator: Sagrada Família (oficial)

events.title: Moves Into Workshop
events.description: In 1925 Antoni Gaudí leaves his house in Park Güell and moves into the Sagrada Família workshop. He lives there to give his time to the church’s construction and religious practice.

images.caption: Reconstructed interior of Gaudí’s Sagrada Família workshop
images.creator: Sagrada Família (oficial)

events.title: Dies After Tram Accident
events.description: On June 7, 1926, a number 30 tram strikes Antoni Gaudí as he walks in Barcelona and leaves him unconscious. Passersby mistake him for a beggar and take him by taxi to Hospital de la Santa Creu. The Sagrada Família chaplain, Mosén Gil Parés, recognizes him the next day. Gaudí’s condition is then too severe for further treatment, and he dies in Barcelona on June 10.

images.caption: Former Hospital de la Santa Creu in Barcelona
images.creator: Zarateman
